beats.label: self-tickle
lines: Why does your own hand feel less ticklish than someone else’s?

beats.text: A tickling robot couldn't make them laugh.
lines: In one MRI study, people used a joystick to control a tickling robot—and still couldn't make themselves laugh.
When you move your hand, the cerebellum predicts the contact and tells the somatosensory cortex what to expect.
An unknown cortical mechanism then reduces the tickle response.

beats.title: Evolutionary hypotheses
lines: One proposed benefit: light touch acts as a “non-self detector,” helping guard against foreign objects.
Ticklish areas may also prompt protection of vulnerable spots.
So try this: close your eyes and touch your nose.
Then let a friend surprise you with a tickle.

sources.claim: Self-tickling fails because self-produced contact is predictable and lacks the unexpected motion needed to activate the tickle response.
In an MRI study using a joystick-controlled tickling robot, participants could not make themselves laugh.
Researchers suggested that the cerebellum sends the somatosensory cortex precise information about expected self-generated sensation, while an unknown cortical mechanism reduces tickling.
Light-touch knismesis may serve as a non-self detector against foreign objects, and ticklish areas may encourage protection of vulnerable body areas.

youtube.title: Why Can't You Tickle Yourself? Surprise Is the Key
youtube.description: Your brain predicts self-generated touch, reducing the surprise that makes tickling ticklish.
